Amanda, it is Rafael. I spoke to the board this morning, and I want to give you the short version before the call with Ingrid. I brought up the six-month idea, and nobody turned it down, which is good news. But the chairman asked a question I could not answer: if the buyer backs out after the site visit, can we sell the credits to somebody else immediately, or do we have to wait? Could you look into that today? The board has also ruled out any discount on the price, so please do not put forward anything that sounds like one. And one more thing: the finance team wants to carry out its own review of the payment dates before we sign. I told them they would have your comments by Thursday. Call me if that is a problem.

A lot of lawyers believe that phrasal verbs are informal, so they avoid them. That is half true. In a contract, you will read that the parties shall conduct an audit, or that the buyer may reject an offer. But in the meeting about that contract, nobody talks like that. People say they will carry out the audit, look into the problem, or turn the offer down. If you only use the formal verbs, you sound like you are reading the agreement out loud. So you need both: the formal verb for the document, and the phrasal verb for the room. One more detail, and it is the one that gives non-native speakers away. With most of these verbs, a pronoun goes in the middle. You draw it up, you turn it down, you rule it out. Never draw up it. And with a few, like look into, the pronoun stays at the end: we are looking into it.

Open the call and say who you are. Then refer to the last meeting. Then go through the first update. Then go through the second update. Then put forward your recommendation. And finally, wrap up and agree the next step.
